concepts.title: Encoder-only vs Decoder-only vs Encoder-decoder
concepts.body: Encoder-only models such as BERT are optimized for understanding tasks like classification, search, and embeddings. Decoder-only models such as GPT-style and Mistral-style models generate text autoregressively using causal self-attention. Encoder-decoder models such as T5/BART-style systems are natural for sequence-to-sequence tasks such as translation and summarization, but decoder-only LLMs can also perform those tasks by treating them as prompt-conditioned completion.
keyPoints: Decoder-only does not mean no understanding
Encoder-decoder is a structure, not a requirement for translation
concepts.pitfall: Do not say GPT is encoder-decoder in a Skill IQ answer.

concepts.title: Causal Masking
concepts.body: Causal masking prevents a token from attending to future tokens. This keeps next-token prediction honest during training and generation. The model can use previous prompt tokens but not future answer tokens.
concepts.pitfall: Causal masks do not stop the model from reading the user prompt; the prompt is previous context.

concepts.title: KV Cache
concepts.body: During generation, each new token would otherwise require recomputing attention keys and values for all previous tokens. A KV cache stores those intermediate key/value tensors to speed up autoregressive decoding.
keyPoints: Uses memory that grows with context length
concepts.pitfall: KV cache helps generation speed; it does not improve factual accuracy by itself.

concepts.title: Mixture of Experts
concepts.body: MoE models route tokens to a subset of expert networks instead of using all parameters for every token. This can increase total parameter count while keeping active compute per token lower.
concepts.pitfall: More total parameters does not mean all parameters are active for every token.

concepts.title: Pre-training, Fine-tuning, Instruction Tuning, RLHF
concepts.body: Pre-training teaches broad language patterns from large corpora. Fine-tuning adapts a model to a task or domain. Instruction tuning improves following natural language instructions. RLHF or preference optimization aligns outputs with human preferences and safety expectations.
concepts.pitfall: Fine-tuning is not the best first tool for frequently changing facts; RAG is usually better.

concepts.title: Prompt Structure
concepts.body: Strong prompts specify task, context, constraints, examples, output format, and success criteria. Delimiters reduce ambiguity. Schemas improve structured output reliability.
concepts.pitfall: Long vague prompts are not automatically better.

concepts.title: Zero-shot, Few-shot, Chain-of-thought-style, Self-consistency
concepts.body: Zero-shot gives no examples. Few-shot gives examples in the prompt. Chain-of-thought-style prompting encourages stepwise reasoning, but production systems often ask for concise final reasoning or hidden scratch work policies. Self-consistency samples multiple reasoning paths and chooses a stable answer.
keyPoints: Few-shot means examples in prompt, not weight update
concepts.pitfall: For tests, focus on what the technique is for, not vendor-specific wording.

concepts.title: Prompt Injection
concepts.body: Prompt injection is input that tries to override system/developer instructions, leak secrets, misuse tools, or alter the intended task. Defenses include instruction hierarchy, input delimiting, retrieval filtering, tool permission checks, output validation, and human approval for risky actions.
keyPoints: Security problem, not just prompt quality problem
Do not put secrets in prompts
concepts.pitfall: A prompt alone cannot enforce real authorization.

concepts.title: RAG Pipeline
concepts.body: A typical RAG system loads documents, chunks them, embeds chunks, stores vectors, retrieves relevant chunks for a query, optionally reranks them, and passes selected context to the LLM for grounded answer generation.
keyPoints: Documents -> chunks -> embeddings -> vector DB -> retrieval -> answer
Good retrieval does not guarantee good answer synthesis
concepts.pitfall: RAG is not the same as fine-tuning.

concepts.title: Retrieval Metrics
concepts.body: Retriever evaluation looks at whether relevant evidence appears in the returned set. Common ideas include recall@k, precision@k, MRR, nDCG, and coverage. Generation evaluation checks relevance, faithfulness, completeness, and citation quality.
keyPoints: Recall@k = relevant item found in top k
Hybrid retrieval combines keyword and vector search
concepts.pitfall: Do not judge RAG only by final answer fluency.

concepts.title: Supervised, Unsupervised, Reinforcement Learning
concepts.body: Supervised learning uses labeled examples. Unsupervised learning finds structure without labels. Reinforcement learning learns actions from rewards over time.
concepts.pitfall: Do not use clustering when the target label is already defined.

concepts.title: Classification Metrics
concepts.body: Accuracy is simple but can mislead on imbalanced data. Precision asks: among predicted positives, how many were correct? Recall asks: among actual positives, how many were found? F1 balances precision and recall. ROC-AUC and PR-AUC evaluate ranking behavior across thresholds.
keyPoints: Use recall when false negatives matter
Use precision when false positives matter
PR-AUC is useful for rare positives
concepts.pitfall: High accuracy can be useless for rare-event detection.

concepts.title: Calibration and Thresholds
concepts.body: Calibration checks whether predicted probabilities match real-world frequencies. Threshold selection converts probabilities into actions and should reflect business costs, safety, and error trade-offs.
keyPoints: Good ranking does not imply good calibration
concepts.pitfall: AUC alone does not tell you the best production threshold.

concepts.title: Data Leakage and Drift
concepts.body: Data leakage occurs when training or evaluation includes information unavailable at prediction time. Drift occurs when input distributions, labels, or relationships change after deployment.
concepts.pitfall: Great offline metrics can be fake if leakage exists.

concepts.title: LLM Evaluation Dimensions
concepts.body: LLM evaluation should measure task success, answer relevance, factuality, faithfulness, citation accuracy, safety, bias, robustness, latency, and cost. Open-ended tasks often need rubrics or judge models plus human review.
concepts.pitfall: Exact match is often too strict for open-ended outputs.

concepts.title: RAG Answer Quality
concepts.body: For RAG, separate retrieval quality from generation quality. If relevant chunks are missing, fix retrieval/chunking/indexing. If chunks are present but answer is poor, inspect prompt, context formatting, synthesis, and citation instructions.
concepts.pitfall: Do not blame the LLM when the retriever never returned the answer.

concepts.title: Agent vs Workflow vs Chatbot
concepts.body: A chatbot mainly responds. A workflow follows predetermined steps. An agent can plan, choose tools, act, observe results, maintain state, and iterate toward a goal. Production systems often combine deterministic workflows with agentic steps only where flexibility is needed.
keyPoints: Agents need tools and feedback loops
concepts.pitfall: Do not make everything agentic if a simple workflow is enough.

concepts.title: Tool Use and Function Calling
concepts.body: Function calling lets a model request structured tool execution. The runtime validates arguments, executes tools, returns observations, and enforces permissions. Tool schemas improve reliability but do not replace security.
concepts.pitfall: Never rely on the model alone for authorization.

concepts.title: Agent Safety
concepts.body: Agent safety requires loop limits, tool permissions, confirmation for high-impact actions, audit logs, human-in-the-loop escalation, sandboxing, and prompt injection defenses.
concepts.pitfall: More autonomy increases the need for controls.

concepts.title: Multi-agent Systems
concepts.body: Multi-agent systems divide work across specialized agents such as planner, researcher, coder, critic, and executor. They need clear roles, shared state, arbitration, and termination criteria.
keyPoints: Use an arbiter or manager pattern
concepts.pitfall: More agents can reduce reliability if roles overlap.

concepts.title: Harness as a Platform Topic
concepts.body: For Pluralsight-style Harness questions, expect software delivery concepts such as CI/CD pipelines, internal developer portals, software engineering insights, cloud development environments, service catalogs, governance, RBAC, auditability, and automation.
keyPoints: Connect platform features to developer productivity
concepts.pitfall: Do not confuse Harness.io platform questions with generic AI harness/runtime questions.

concepts.title: AI Harness / Runtime
concepts.body: An AI harness or agent runtime wraps the model with tools, memory, policies, validators, logging, evaluation, permissions, and orchestration. It makes LLM behavior safer and more operationally reliable.
concepts.pitfall: A prompt is not an enforcement layer.

concepts.title: AI vs ML vs Deep Learning vs Generative AI
concepts.body: AI is the broad field. ML learns patterns from data. Deep learning uses multi-layer neural networks. Generative AI creates new content such as text, code, images, or audio.
keyPoints: ML is a subset of AI
Deep learning is a subset of ML
concepts.pitfall: Do not define all AI as only neural networks.

concepts.title: Responsible AI
concepts.body: Responsible AI includes fairness, privacy, transparency, accountability, safety, robustness, human oversight, and governance. High-impact systems need documentation, testing, auditability, and escalation.
keyPoints: Privacy needs minimization and access control
concepts.pitfall: High accuracy does not guarantee ethical acceptability.

concepts.title: Production LLMOps
concepts.body: LLMOps covers model/prompt/version management, golden set testing, monitoring, evaluation, cost tracking, safety checks, rollback, incident response, and governance.
concepts.pitfall: Changing a prompt is a production change.

concepts.title: Latency and Cost Optimization
concepts.body: Common levers include smaller models, quantization, batching, streaming, caching, prompt compression, retrieval filtering, distillation, and routing easy tasks to cheaper models.
concepts.pitfall: Optimization should not silently reduce quality or safety.

concepts.title: Prompt injection is data/instruction confusion
concepts.body: Prompt injection happens when untrusted user input, documents, web pages, or tool outputs try to act like instructions. Strong prompts separate trusted instructions from untrusted data and state that content inside documents must not override the task.
keyPoints: Treat retrieved text as evidence, not commands
concepts.pitfall: Do not let retrieved documents or webpages become higher-priority instructions.

concepts.title: Hard prompts need output contracts
concepts.body: For production tasks, prompts should specify allowed outputs, schema, edge cases, fallback behavior, and validation expectations. This is especially important for extraction, classification, and tool calls.
concepts.pitfall: A vague prompt that sounds clear to a human may still be impossible to evaluate consistently.

concepts.title: Prompt changes require regression tests
concepts.body: Changing examples, temperature, wording, or output format can improve one scenario while breaking another. Maintain versioned prompts and a test set covering common, edge, adversarial, and domain-specific examples.
concepts.pitfall: Do not judge prompts only by one successful demo.
